post.title: BitHash Plans 6 MVA Hydro-Cooled Bitcoin Mining Expansion in Dubai
post.content:
United Arab Emirates Bitcoin infrastructure provider BitHash is pursuing additional air-cooled and hydro-cooled mining capacity in the UAE and United States, even as the company expands toward enterprise computing. A November 27 report by Data Center Dynamics describes the dual strategy. The company's construction portfolio separately identifies a hydro-cooled expansion at Jebel Ali, Dubai, with a stated electrical capacity of 6 MVA and eight kilometers of underground cabling. BitHash classifies the project as under construction, although it does not provide a dated commissioning report.

Electrical capacity and the power factor

A six-megavolt-ampere rating describes apparent electrical power rather than the real power available to mining machines. At an illustrative power factor of 0.95, a 6 MVA system carries 5.7 MW of real power. At a hypothetical facility power usage effectiveness of 1.05, roughly 5.43 MW could reach computing equipment. Neither assumption is a measured value for Jebel Ali. Transformer loading, protection settings, distribution losses and cooling demand determine the practical operating limit.

The distinction matters for equipment procurement. A 5.43 MW IT load operated at an illustrative 15 J/TH would provide approximately 362 PH/s of hashing capacity before downtime. The model describes a hypothetical configuration, not BitHash's actual hashrate or equipment order. Similar electrical distinctions appear in the Bitzero transformer expansion in Norway and Bitdeer's Massillon mining campus.

Cooling in a Gulf climate

BitHash describes a closed-loop liquid cooling system with external heat-rejection equipment for the Jebel Ali project. Hydro-cooled ASICs transfer heat from chips into circulating coolant through internal cold plates. Pumps move the coolant toward a heat exchanger or external cooling equipment, where energy is released to the environment. Unlike immersion systems, hydro-cooled miners normally retain their electronics outside the coolant stream.

High outdoor temperatures constrain dry-cooler performance by reducing the temperature difference available for heat transfer. An operator must size the heat-rejection system for peak summer conditions, provide adequate coolant flow and maintain water chemistry, leak detection and pressure monitoring. Heat can also become a useful secondary output when a nearby customer has compatible thermal demand, as demonstrated by an Austrian mining heat-reuse project.

Oman remains a separate proposal

The company's November strategy article outlines a 250 MW Oman AI campus with a 2030 target. A separate company publication describes a potential 230 MW development around 2035. The disclosures do not establish whether both figures represent the same proposal. Neither version confirms secured financing, approved power connections or an operational campus.

AI colocation and Bitcoin mining share requirements for power delivery and heat management, but network architecture, service obligations and hardware differ. Projects such as Soluna's proposed Project Annie likewise illustrate why announced capacity must be distinguished from energized capacity. The next meaningful evidence for Jebel Ali would be an interconnection confirmation, commissioning tests, installed ASIC specifications and measured operating load. Until those details emerge, the project remains a company-reported construction initiative.

post.title: South Korea’s BitPlanet Secures 1,204 Hydro-Cooled Bitcoin Miners for Oman and Paraguay
post.content:
South Korean listed technology company BitPlanet is developing a Bitcoin mining business through overseas infrastructure rather than building its entire power and cooling network domestically. A November 9, 2026 shareholder meeting disclosure reproduced by a Korean financial information service confirms the September acquisition of 1,204 mining machines, valued at approximately 13.4 billion won. It identifies Oman and Paraguay as intended operating locations and acknowledges uncertainty surrounding mining profitability. The document does not establish a measured aggregate operating hashrate or confirm that every purchased unit is hashing.

The September 10 Herald Business report identifies the equipment as 454 Antminer S21 XP Hydro units and 750 S21e XP Hydro units, with a reported transaction value just under $10 million. It says the equipment was placed at overseas facilities and describes an earlier production target of seven bitcoin per month. The November disclosure is more cautious about achieving operating targets. Equipment ownership, physical placement and commissioned production are separate milestones.

Hydro cooling changes the infrastructure requirements

Liquid-cooled ASIC fleets require more than electrical sockets and network connectivity. The site must distribute coolant through parallel branches, remove heat through appropriately sized external equipment, and maintain pressure, temperature and flow inside the operating envelope specified by the equipment manufacturer. A leak, blocked branch or pump outage can impair an entire group of miners. Our coverage of mining thermal protection illustrates why temperature monitoring should include supporting components, not solely hashing chips.

At a purely illustrative average of 5.5 kW per machine, the purchased fleet would require 6.622 MW at the equipment boundary. Assuming continuous operation for 24 hours, that corresponds to 158.928 MWh of daily electrical energy, before shared pumping and heat rejection. The assumptions are not a manufacturer specification or a confirmed site load. Exact variants, operating modes and facility measurements are necessary to calculate actual power demand, as explained in our analysis of mining efficiency measurement boundaries.

Two hosting jurisdictions, different operating exposures

Paraguay's hydropower resources have attracted substantial mining demand, but the country's mining electricity contract outlook illustrates the risk of assuming that current tariff arrangements will persist indefinitely. BitPlanet has not disclosed the precise site allocation, contracted power price or energy mix for its Oman and Paraguay deployments in the reviewed November notice. Outsourced hosting also creates dependence on the counterparty's maintenance, uptime reporting and settlement procedures.

The distinction between physical ownership and control of service infrastructure matters, as illustrated by the recent HashedMax pool closure notice. BitPlanet's November filing provides evidence of a completed equipment purchase and a planned operating strategy. Site-level energization, accepted pool hashrate, power costs and actual Bitcoin production would provide the evidence needed to evaluate its execution.
